content: The prevalence of opioid use among pregnant women varies widely, ranging from 1% to 2% in some populations to as high as 21% in others. In the United States, opioid use among pregnant women delivering in hospitals increased fourfold between 1999 and 2014. Heroin readily crosses the placenta, and opioid dependence during pregnancy is associated with a sixfold increase in maternal obstetric complications. These complications include low birth weight, preeclampsia, third-trimester bleeding, abnormal fetal positioning, postpartum infections, fetal distress, and meconium aspiration. Neonates born to opioid-dependent mothers are at risk for withdrawal symptoms, impaired postnatal growth, microcephaly, neurobehavioral issues, increased neonatal mortality, and a significantly elevated risk (74-fold) of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). This updated Cochrane Review, originally published in 2008 and last updated in 2013, aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of maintenance treatments for opioid-dependent pregnant women. The review assessed the impact of these treatments, alone or in combination with psychosocial interventions, on child health outcomes, neonatal mortality, treatment retention, and substance use reduction. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated pharmacological maintenance treatments for opioid-dependent pregnant women. Four trials involving 271 pregnant women were identified. Three trials compared methadone with buprenorphine, while one compared methadone with oral slow-release morphine. Three of the four studies had adequate allocation concealment and were double-blinded. However, a significant limitation was the high dropout rate (30% to 40%) in three of the studies, which was unevenly distributed between treatment groups. Methadone versus Buprenorphine: There was likely no significant difference in treatment dropout rates between methadone and buprenorphine (risk ratio [RR] 0.66, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.37 to 1.20; moderate-quality evidence). There may be no significant difference in the use of primary substances between the two treatments (RR 1.81, 95% CI 0.70 to 4.68; low-quality evidence). Birth weight may be higher in the buprenorphine group, as reported in two trials. One trial found a mean difference (MD) of -530.00 g (95% CI -662.78 to -397.22; 19 participants), and another reported an MD of -215.00 g (95% CI -238.93 to -191.07; 131 participants). However, the results could not be pooled due to high heterogeneity, and the evidence quality was very low. There may be no significant difference in APGAR scores between the two groups (MD 0.00, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.03; low-quality evidence). Neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS) was assessed using various measures. The number of newborns treated for NAS may not differ significantly between groups (RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.63; low-quality evidence). One study reported side effects, finding no significant difference in the number of mothers experiencing serious adverse events (RR 1.69, 95% CI 0.75 to 3.83; low-quality evidence) or newborns with serious adverse events (RR 4.77, 95% CI 0.59 to 38.49; low-quality evidence). Methadone versus Slow-Release Morphine: No participants dropped out in either treatment group. Oral slow-release morphine may be more effective than methadone in promoting abstinence from heroin use during pregnancy (RR 2.40, 95% CI 1.00 to 5.77; low-quality evidence). No maternal side effects were reported in this comparison. However, one neonate in the methadone group experienced central apnea, while one neonate in the morphine group experienced obstructive apnea (low-quality evidence). Conclusions: Methadone and buprenorphine appear to have similar efficacy and safety profiles for treating opioid dependence in pregnant women and their infants. However, there is insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about the comparison between methadone and slow-release morphine. Overall, the evidence base is too limited to make definitive conclusions about the equivalence of these treatments. Further randomized controlled trials with larger sample sizes are needed to compare different maintenance treatments.
